# Check it against real life

## A real bouncing ball, photographed 25 times a second

![A stroboscopic photograph of a ball bouncing across a floor, each flash a fixed time apart](asset:strobe_ball)

The flashes are evenly spaced in time, so the distance between two images is pure spacing. Compare the gaps near the floor with those near the top of each bounce, then with your chart.

## A bouncing ball to critique

![A beach ball bouncing in a simple short loop](asset:beach_ball_loop)

It was made to show off a file format, not weight. Using this week's words, name what is missing.

## Motion, measured: an early landmark

![Muybridge's galloping horse, eleven photographs played as a loop](asset:horse_in_motion)

In 1878 a row of cameras photographed a galloping horse, one frame each. It took a team: Leland Stanford paid for it, the photographer Eadweard Muybridge staged it and patented the method, railroad engineers built the camera triggers, and a jockey, named on the card only as G. Domm, rode the horse.

{{microscope:who-made-the-horse-move}}

{{deeper}}

**None of these was made for this course.** Each is a real, public, credited work.

**The strobe ball, looked at closely.** Compare the widest gap near the floor with the narrowest gap near the top of an arc. That difference is what your assignment needs. Look at the shape just after each bounce, too. The real ball wobbles out of round.

**The beach ball, if you are stuck.** Watch where it is slow and where it is fast. If you can say what you would change, and why, you have the week's main idea.

**The horse, the whole story.** The run was at a track in Palo Alto, California. Twelve cameras fired one after another as the horse ran past, and settled an argument: do all four hooves ever leave the ground at once? They do. The loop shows eleven photographs, fewer than your 12 drawings, and it still reads as a gallop. (Twelve cameras fired; this loop uses frames 1 to 11, as its Commons record says.) Watch what the eleventh frame does to join back up to the first.

Muybridge usually gets the credit alone, and credit was fought over at the time in both directions. You may hear that the photographs settled a $25,000 bet. Nobody has ever found a record of that bet. What the photographs proved is that motion can be measured instead of described. This week you did the same thing in miniature: fix the interval, decide where the object is at each one, and let the eye do the rest.
